newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Waigel accuses forex markets of overreaction.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Waigel accuses forex markets of overreaction.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Tuesday Bonn wanted to see a strong mark and that the present strength of sterling and the dollar against the German currency was due to overreaction by financial markets.
Waigel's comments briefly sent both the British and U.S. currencies lower against the mark but they quickly bounced back.

The finance minister's remarks came a few days after Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer also briefly halted the dollar's grinding advance when he said he thought the U.S. unit's rise from its historic lows of 1995 had finished.

"We are interested in a strong deutschemark. I think what's happening at the moment is an overreaction of the markets," Waigel told a news conference in Berlin in response to a question about the strength of the dollar and pound.
"We have, as in the past, agreed cooperation within the G7," he added. "We are in contact with our partners."
Waigel also declined to comment specifically on France's efforts to meet criteria for Europe's single currency, saying simply that all candidate countries had to do their homework.

France's Socialist-led government has raised doubts about its ability to meet the fiscal criteria for economic and monetary union (EMU), particularly the budget deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product.
Waigel, speaking during a visit to Berlin with other leaders from his Christian Social Union party, did not name any economic fundamental reasons why he thought the mark was undervalued.
If his remarks were intended to stop the dollar in its tracks, they are unlikely to please German exporters, who have been reaping big benefits from the strong U.S. currency.
The trend has also boosted the equity market, with exporting stocks driving Germany's DAX share index 44 percent higher since the start of the year.
Both the dollar and the pound steadied after a brief dip on Waigel's remarks and more than made up their lost ground.
At 1200 GMT, the dollar was quoted at 1.7945 compared with 1.7927 in late Monday trade and the pound surged to 3.0240 marks, just above its 3.0237 six-year high achieved on Monday.
The Bundesbank declined to comment on market speculation that it was checking mark prices in the foreign exchange market.
Currency dealers earlier said the central bank was checking mark prices but there were no reports of concrete action.

Asked about France's chances of meeting the EMU criteria, Waigel said "There are clear targets and clear agreements... Every country has the chance and the obligation to do their bit in 1997 to meet the criteria."
He said all countries, including France, had made clear it was up to each country to concentrate on their own homework to prepare for the new currency, due to be launched at the beginning of 1999.
"We're doing that and so are others," he said. "I'm not evaluating the efforts of others."
